summary: Deep-sea life for ages 9–11 across three ideas: (1) bioluminescence — some deep animals chemically produce their own light to lure prey, find mates, or startle/hide from predators (including counter-illumination); (2) adaptations to total darkness and crushing pressure — huge eyes or none, soft water-filled bodies with no air spaces, big mouths, slow metabolism; (3) the paradigm shift — hydrothermal vent communities thrive on chemical energy from the vent, not sunlight, overturning the idea that every food web starts with sunlight. Keep mechanism at 'chemical energy instead of sunlight'; full chemosynthesis chemistry comes later (KS3). Tie each adaptation to a specific challenge, and keep making-light (a survival tool) distinct from the vent's energy source.
misconceptions: 'Nothing can live that deep' — not knowing the deep sea teems with specially adapted life.
'All life ultimately depends on sunlight' — the key misconception overturned by chemosynthetic vent communities.
'Bioluminescence is reflected/leftover sunlight' — rather than light the animal actively produces chemically.
'Deep-sea animals would be crushed' — not understanding soft, water-filled bodies with no air spaces resist pressure.
'The vent food web is powered by the vent's heat' — conflating heat with the chemical energy bacteria actually use.

activities.title: Tap the dark: creatures that make their own light
steps: Start in an almost completely black 'midnight zone' deep-sea scene where you can barely see anything.

Tap or point to spots in the darkness; where a creature hides, its OWN light switches on to reveal it — e.g. an anglerfish's lure flickers, a jelly pulses electric blue, a shoal of lanternfish sparkles.
For each revealed creature, open the explanation flap and read WHY it glows (lure prey / find a mate / startle or hide from predators) and HOW it survives darkness and pressure.
State in your own words what bioluminescence means, and give one job the light does for a named deep-sea animal.
Watch real deep-sea footage (anglerfish lure, lanternfish, glowing jellies) if available, to see living light in a lightless world.
activities.insight: Below about 1000 m no sunlight reaches, so many deep animals actively make their own light chemically — bioluminescence is a survival tool, not reflected or leftover sunlight.

activities.title: Adaptation to challenge: equip a creature for the deep
steps: List the three main challenges of the deep: total darkness, crushing pressure from kilometres of water, and scarce food.

For a deep-sea creature, choose adaptations and justify each against a challenge: e.g. huge eyes OR a light organ for darkness; a soft, water-filled body with no air spaces for pressure; a big mouth and slow metabolism for scarce food.
If an equip-and-test builder is available, select a light organ / eye type / body type / mouth, then test whether the creature survives, and revise choices that fail.
Explain why a soft, water-filled body with no air spaces resists crushing pressure, rather than being crushed as a gas-filled surface fish would be.

Rank the hazards: the deep sea is both cold and under crushing pressure, but note that crushing pressure is the dominant and most-underestimated challenge — and that hydrothermal vents are actually hot, not freezing.
activities.insight: Each deep-sea feature is a response to a specific environmental challenge; soft bodies with no air spaces survive pressure. The deep is genuinely cold, but crushing pressure is the dominant, commonly-overlooked hazard — while vents themselves are hot.

activities.title: Life without sunlight: the hydrothermal vent surprise
steps: First establish the familiar rule: surface food webs start with plants/algae using sunlight (photosynthesis).
Find a shimmering plume of hot, mineral-rich water (a 'black smoker') on the dark seafloor and drill in to a hydrothermal vent surrounded by thriving tube worms, clams and crabs.
Open the contrast flap/panel comparing a surface food web (base = sunlight) with a vent food web (base = chemical energy from the vent).
Build or label the vent food web by placing chemical-energy-using bacteria at the BASE instead of sunlight, then the animals that live on them.
Answer: 'What powers a vent community?' and explain in your own words that a food web needs an energy source but it need not be sunlight.
Distinguish the vent's HEAT from the CHEMICAL energy the bacteria actually use — heat is not what feeds the food web.
activities.insight: An ecosystem needs an energy source, but it need not be sunlight: at vents, bacteria use chemical energy from vent fluids as the base of a food web supporting tube worms, clams and crabs — so life can thrive where no sunlight ever reaches.

checkQuestion: Right at the bottom of the deep ocean, in total darkness where no sunlight ever reaches, there are whole communities of animals living around hot cracks in the seafloor called hydrothermal vents. A child says 'that can't be right — nothing can live with no sunlight, because all food comes from plants that need the Sun'. What would you tell them, and how can a food web start with no sunlight at all?
checkAnswer: Life really does thrive there. Not all food webs start with sunlight: at hydrothermal vents, tiny bacteria make food using chemical energy from the minerals and hot gases pouring out of the vents (not light), and animals like tube worms and vent crabs live on those bacteria. So the base of that food web is chemical energy, not sunlight. Deep-sea animals also cope with darkness and crushing pressure using adaptations — many make their own light (bioluminescence) to lure prey, find mates or hide, and their bodies are built to withstand the pressure.
